message.reasoning:
I am evaluating a trade offer in Monopoly.

The offer swaps ST_JAMES_PLACE for $40 and CONNECTICUT_AVENUE. I would gain two light blue properties but lose St. James Place. The opponent would then hold Tennessee and St. James Place.

This is the same offer structure as the rejected turn 8 swap. I previously rejected it because it was -$40 face value and gave the opponent two-thirds of the orange set while I only gained two-thirds cheap light blues.

The net value is still $20 below list. I will reject this offer. It gives the opponent two-thirds of the orange set and leaves New York unowned.

I will not counter this offer. A higher bid would signal that St. James Place is buyable. I have no counter that helps me without giving the opponent another orange property.

I am reconsidering a cash-only counter for Connecticut. I would offer $200 to $240 for that property alone, without giving up St. James Place.

I rejected the cash-only counter for Connecticut. The opponent already refused that offer at turn 8, and paying $200 would waste an exchange while signaling interest in the property.

This is a fresh trade proposal rather than a continuation of the previous rejected offer. I can counter it.

The opponent frames the deal as symmetric, but giving up St. James Place is the worst possible move. Oranges are the strongest color group, and Park Place must never go to them.

I am weighing whether to reject this offer cleanly or attempt a cash-only counter for Connecticut.

The offer is not symmetric in value. Oranges are far more powerful than light blues, and I already hold one orange property while the opponent holds two. My St. James Place is a denial asset that blocks them from completing the orange set; it cannot help me build an orange monopoly because I lack the other two oranges.

I will reject this offer outright. A cash counter for Connecticut would keep the negotiation open and risk letting them extract St. James Place later. I will not signal that St. James is buyable.
